Digital pass-though works just fine in Linux. Now the question would be does the card have drivers for Linux, most do. asus, you're good.

There are of course a dozen different options on how to put sound to the card. Using Alsa, just the raw driver, means that it'll work with the least amount of fuss. There is Pulse-Audio, which most distributions include, which will reroute and enable plugins before handing it off to the card. Pulse-Audio also enables using non-standard cards, DAC over Firewire and virtual cards. This can be used to pipe anything into a non-standard DAC or whatever. However only if you are also going to be recording, the low-latency toolkit is a PITA to setup, includes hundreds of options, and generally is overkill, is the jack-audio-connection-kit. It includes the most options, but isn't designed to be easy.

You don't loose capacity. What happens is Linux loves caching data from the hard drive. If you have 8 gigs and are only using 1, linux might use 6 gigs to cache just in case you want to access that data again (which will be much faster from RAM than hard drive). That 6 gigs is only used for caching as long as nothing else needs it. So it looks like you only have 1 gig free but in reality you have 7 gigs available.

The one area where you might loose something is with your graphics card. Linux GPU drivers are less efficient atm but that's starting to change. It's mostly going to be an imperceptible difference but you will have slightly smoother sailing if you have an Nvidia card.

How good is it, really, for gaming? I have a shit load of games. I will be upset if they cannot install.

Compatibility might be a problem. A lot of older games and AAA games do not natively support Linux. But there are a surprisingly amount of AAA games that do. If you primarily play through steam just look for Steam OS support.

Games that do support linux natively tend to, IME, run better. USUALLY you're going to have a lot less bloat wear on a linux OS so there's less for your computer to do. And if anything does break it's far easier to find out what happened and get help on Linux than on Windows.

edit: tl;dr: Compatibility with some games is the dealbreaker. The GPU drivers can be a bit of a pain but it's usually not a big deal. Everything else is awesome.
